Diệu Âm | tagalog_name = Mangushli | cebuano_name = Mangushli | veneration = {{ill|Mahayana|en|Mahayana|WD=Q48362|lt=Mahayana}}, {{ill|Vajrayana|en|Vajrayana|WD=Q172175|lt=Vajrayana}} | attributes = | shakti = | preceded_by = | succeeded_by = }} '''Manjushri''' ({{langx|sa|मञ्जुश्री|Mañjuśrī}}) is a ''{{ill|Bodhisattva|en|Bodhisattva|WD=Q178149|lt=Bodhisattva}}'' who represents ''{{ill|Prajñā (Buddhism)|en|Prajñā (Buddhism)|WD=Q849649|lt=prajñā}}'' (transcendent wisdom) of the Buddhas in [[:en:Mahāyāna Buddhism|Mahāyāna Buddhism]]. The name "Mañjuśrī" is a combination of Sanskrit word "" and an honorific "[[:en:śrī|śrī]]"; it can be literally translated as "Beautiful One with Glory" or "Beautiful One with Auspiciousness". Mañjuśrī is also known by the fuller name of Mañjuśrīkumārabhūta ({{lang|sa|मञ्जुश्रीकुमारभूत}}),Keown, Damien (editor) with Hodge, Stephen; Jones, Charles; Tinti, Paola (2003). ''A Dictionary of Buddhism.'' Oxford, UK: Oxford University Press. {{ISBN|0-19-860560-9}} p.172. literally "Mañjuśrī, Still a Youth" or, less literally, "Prince Mañjuśrī". Another name of Mañjuśrī is Mañjughoṣa. ==In Mahāyāna Buddhism== [[File:Manjushri statue. Lalung Gompa, Spiti.jpg|thumb|left|200px|Manjushri statue, Lhalung Gompa, [[:en:Spiti Valley|Spiti Valley]], India]] [[File:Manjushri at Buddha Tooth Relic Temple and Museum.JPG|thumb|200px|Manjushri, seated on a blue lion at {{ill|Buddha Tooth Relic Temple and Museum|en|Buddha Tooth Relic Temple and Museum|WD=Q839965|lt=Buddha Tooth Relic Temple and Museum}}, {{ill|Singapore|en|Singapore|WD=Q334|lt=Singapore}}.]] [[File:The Bodhisattva Monju (Manjushri), Kamakura period, Japan.jpg|thumb|200px|Bodhisattva Monju (Manjushri), {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period}}, {{ill|Tokyo National Museum|en|Tokyo National Museum|WD=Q653433|lt=Tokyo National Museum}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan}}]] Scholars have identified Mañjuśrī as the oldest and most significant bodhisattva in Mahāyāna literature.A View of Manjushri: Wisdom and Its Crown Prince in Pala Period India. Harrington, Laura. Doctoral Thesis, Columbia University, 2002 Mañjuśrī is first referred to in early [[:en:Mahāyāna sūtras|Mahāyāna sūtras]] such as the [[:en:Prajñāpāramitā|Prajñāpāramitā]] ''sūtra''s and through this association, very early in the tradition he came to symbolize the embodiment of ''prajñā'' (transcendent wisdom). The ''{{ill|en:Lotus Sutra|en|en:Lotus Sutra|WD=Q861212|lt=en:Lotus Sutra}}'' assigns him a [[:en:Pure land|Pure land]] called ''Vimala'', which according to the ''{{ill|Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra|en|Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra|WD=Q790258|lt=Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra}}'' is located in the East. His pure land is predicted to be one of the two best pure lands in all of existence in all the past, present, and future. When he attains {{ill|Buddhahood|en|Buddhahood|WD=Q56247062|lt=Buddhahood}} his name will be Universal Sight{{Citation needed|date=September 2022}}. In the ''Lotus Sūtra'', Mañjuśrī also leads the {{ill|en:Longnü|en|en:Longnü|WD=Q6674175|lt=Nagaraja's daughter}} to enlightenment. He also figures in the ''[[:en:Vimalakīrti Sūtra|Vimalakīrti Sūtra]]'' in a debate with [[:en:Vimalakīrti|Vimalakīrti]] where he is presented as a Bodhisattva who discusses non-duality with him. An example of a wisdom teaching of Mañjuśrī can be found in the ''Saptaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra'' ({{ill|Taishō Tripiṭaka|en|Taishō Tripiṭaka|WD=Q837315|lt=Taishō Tripiṭaka}} 232).{{citation|url=http://www.acmuller.net/descriptive_catalogue/files/k0010.html|title=The Korean Buddhist Canon: A Descriptive Catalog (T 232)}} This ''sūtra'' contains a dialogue between Mañjuśrī and the Buddha on the One [[:en:Samādhi|Samādhi]] (Skt. ''Ekavyūha Samādhi''). {{ill|Sheng-yen|en|Sheng-yen|WD=Q712896|lt=Sheng-yen}} renders the following teaching of Mañjuśrī, for entering ''samādhi'' naturally through transcendent wisdom: {{quote|Contemplate the five {{ill|Skandha|en|Skandha|WD=Q747858|lt=Skandha}}s as originally empty and quiescent, non-arising, non-perishing, equal, without differentiation. Constantly thus practicing, day or night, whether sitting, walking, standing or lying down, finally one reaches an inconceivable state without any obstruction or form. This is the Samadhi of One Act ({{zh|c=一行三昧|p=Yīxíng sānmèi|labels=no}}).Sheng-Yen, Master (聖嚴法師)(1988). [https://web.archive.org/web/20121011012531/http://ccbs.ntu.edu.tw/FULLTEXT/JR-BJ001/02_10.htm ''Tso-Ch'an''], p.364}} ==Vajrayāna Buddhism== Within [[:en:Vajrayāna|Vajrayāna]] Buddhism, Mañjuśrī is a meditational deity and considered a fully enlightened Buddha. In {{ill|Shingon Buddhism|en|Shingon Buddhism|WD=Q550182|lt=Shingon Buddhism}}, he is one of the {{ill|Thirteen Buddhas|en|Thirteen Buddhas|WD=Q3538361|lt=Thirteen Buddhas}} to whom disciples devote themselves. He figures extensively in many esoteric texts such as the ''[[:en:Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa|Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa]]'' and the ''{{ill|Mañjuśrīnāmasamgīti|en|Mañjuśrīnāmasamgīti|WD=Q3577095|lt=Mañjuśrīnāmasamgīti}}''. His consort in some traditions is [[Saraswati]]. The ''Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa'', which later came to be classified under [[Outer Tantras#Kriyatantra|Kriyātantra]], states that ''mantra''s taught in the [[:en:Śaiva|Śaiva]], Garuḍa, and [[:en:Vaiṣṇava|Vaiṣṇava]] ''tantra''s will be effective if applied by Buddhists since they were all taught originally by Mañjuśrī.Sanderson, Alexis. "The Śaiva Age: The Rise and Dominance of Śaivism during the Early Medieval Period." In: Genesis and Development of Tantrism, edited by Shingo Einoo. Tokyo: Institute of Oriental Culture, University of Tokyo, 2009. Institute of Oriental Culture Special Series, 23, pp. 129-131. ==Iconography== Mañjuśrī is depicted as a male bodhisattva wielding a flaming sword in his right hand, representing the realization of transcendent wisdom which cuts down ignorance and duality. The scripture supported by the [[:en:Padma (attribute)|padma]] (lotus) held in his left hand is a ''Prajñāpāramitā sūtra'', representing his attainment of ultimate realization from the blossoming of wisdom. Mañjuśrī is often depicted as riding or seated on a blue {{ill|Lion|en|Lion|WD=Q140|lt=Lion}}, as can be seen at {{ill|Buddha Tooth Relic Temple and Museum|en|Buddha Tooth Relic Temple and Museum|WD=Q839965|lt=Buddha Tooth Relic Temple and Museum}} in {{ill|Singapore|en|Singapore|WD=Q334|lt=Singapore}}. (see opposite), or sitting on the skin of a lion. This represents the use of wisdom to tame the mind, which is compared to riding or subduing a ferocious lion. In Chinese and Japanese Buddhist art, Mañjuśrī's sword is sometimes replaced with a ''{{ill|Ruyi (scepter)|en|Ruyi (scepter)|WD=Q1448880|lt=ruyi}}'' scepter, especially in representations of his ''{{ill|Vimalakirti Sutra|en|Vimalakirti Sutra|WD=Q110646|lt=Vimalakirti Sutra}}'' discussion with the layman {{ill|Vimalakirti|en|Vimalakirti|WD=Q2502143|lt=Vimalakirti}}.Davidson, J. LeRoy, "The Origin and Early Use of the Ju-i", ''Artibus Asiae'' 1950,13.4, 240. According to {{ill|Berthold Laufer|en|Berthold Laufer|WD=Q71600|lt=Berthold Laufer}}, the first Chinese representation of a ''ruyi'' was in an 8th-century Mañjuśrī painting by {{ill|Wu Daozi|en|Wu Daozi|WD=Q1196022|lt=Wu Daozi}}, showing it held in his right hand taking the place of the usual sword. In subsequent Chinese and Japanese paintings of Buddhas, a ''ruyi'' was occasionally represented as a Padma with a long stem curved like a ''ruyi''.Laufer, Berthold, ''[https://openlibrary.org/books/OL7181158M/Jade Jade, a Study in Chinese Archaeology and Religion]'', Field Museum of Natural History, 1912, 339. He is one of the Four Great Bodhisattvas of {{ill|Chinese Buddhism|en|Chinese Buddhism|WD=Q847618|lt=Chinese Buddhism}}, the other three being {{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|Kṣitigarbha|WD=Q604687|lt=Kṣitigarbha}}, {{ill|Avalokiteśvara|en|Avalokiteśvara|WD=Q193849|lt=Avalokiteśvara}}, and {{ill|Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|en|Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|WD=Q868306|lt=Samantabhadra}}. In China, he is often paired with Samantabhadra{{Citation needed|date=September 2022}}. In {{ill|Tibetan Buddhism|en|Tibetan Buddhism|WD=Q483889|lt=Tibetan Buddhism}}, Mañjuśrī is sometimes depicted in a trinity with Avalokiteśvara and [[:en:Vajrapāṇi|Vajrapāṇi]]{{Citation needed|date=September 2022}}. ==Mantras== === Arapacana mantra === A {{ill|Mantra|en|Mantra|WD=Q131510|lt=Mantra}} commonly associated with Mañjuśrī is the following:Buswell, Robert. Lopez, Donald. ''The Princeton Dictionary of Buddhism.'' 2013. p. 527 :''oṃ arapacana dhīḥ'' The Arapacana is a {{ill|Syllabary|en|Syllabary|WD=Q182133|lt=Syllabary}} consisting of forty-two letters, and is named after the first five letters: ''a, ra, pa, ca, na''.Buswell, Robert. Lopez, Donald. ''The Princeton Dictionary of Buddhism.'' 2013. p. 61 This syllabary was most widely used for the [[:en:Gāndhārī language|Gāndhārī language]] with the {{ill|Kharosthi|en|Kharosthi|WD=Q1161266|lt=Kharoṣṭhī script}} but also appears in some Sanskrit texts. The syllabary features in Mahāyāna texts such as the longer ''[[:en:Prajñāpāramitā|Prajñāpāramitā]]'' texts, the ''[[:en:Gaṇḍavyūha Sūtra|Gaṇḍavyūha Sūtra]]'', the ''{{ill|Lalitavistara Sūtra|en|Lalitavistara Sūtra|WD=Q1381826|lt=Lalitavistara Sūtra}}'', the ''[[:en:Avataṃsaka Sūtra|Avataṃsaka Sūtra]]'', the ''{{ill|Dharmaguptaka|en|Dharmaguptaka|WD=Q2445824|lt=Dharmaguptaka}} {{ill|Vinaya|en|Vinaya|WD=Q848764|lt=Vinaya}}'', and the ''[[:en:Mūlasarvāstivāda|Mūlasarvāstivāda]] Vinaya''. In some of these texts, the Arapacana syllabary serves as a {{ill|Mnemonic|en|Mnemonic|WD=Q191062|lt=Mnemonic}} for important Mahāyāna concepts. Due to its association with him, ''Arapacana'' may even serve as an alternate name for Mañjuśrī. The ''Sutra on Perfect Wisdom'' (Conze 1975) defines the significance of each syllable thus: # ''A'' is a door to the insight that all dharmas are unproduced from the very beginning (''ādya-anutpannatvād''). # ''RA'' is a door to the insight that all dharmas are without dirt (''rajas''). # ''PA'' is a door to the insight that all dharmas have been expounded in the ultimate sense (''paramārtha''). # ''CA'' is a door to the insight that the decrease (''cyavana'') or rebirth of any dharma cannot be apprehended, because all dharmas do not decrease, nor are they reborn. # ''NA'' is a door to the insight that the names (i.e. ''nāma'') of all dharmas have vanished; the essential nature behind names cannot be gained or lost. Tibetan pronunciation is slightly different and so the Tibetan characters read: ''{{IAST|oṃ a ra pa tsa na dhīḥ}}'' ({{bo|w=om a ra pa tsa na d+hIH|t=ༀ་ཨ་ར་པ་ཙ་ན་དྷཱི༔|lang=yes}}).[http://www.visiblemantra.org/manjusri.html] - Visible Mantra's website In Tibetan tradition, this mantra is believed to enhance wisdom and improve one's skills in debating, memory, writing, and other literary abilities. "{{IAST|Dhīḥ}}" is the seed syllable of the mantra and is chanted with greater emphasis and also repeated a number of times as a [[:en:decrescendo|decrescendo]]. === Other mantras === According to the {{ill|Mañjuśrī-mūla-kalpa|en|Mañjuśrī-mūla-kalpa|WD=Q6799169|lt=''Mañjuśrī­mūlakalpa''}}, "the ultimate heart essence of Mañjuśrī, which accomplishes all endeavors" is the following mantra:{{Cite web |title=The Root Manual of the Rites of Mañjuśrī / 84000 Reading Room |url=https://read.84000.co/translation/toh543.html |access-date=2024-03-22 |website=84000 Translating The Words of The Buddha |language=en}}
Namaḥ sarvabuddhānām oṁ maṁ
The ''Sādhanamālā'' also contains a popular mantra which refers to Mañjuśrī as the "lord of speech" (Vāgīśvara):Bhattacharyya, Benoytosh. ''The Indian Buddhist Iconography Mainly Based on the Sādhanamālā and Other Cognate Tāntric Texts of Rituals'' (2nd Ed.)'','' pp. 113, 116. K. L. MUKHOPADHYAY, Calcutta, 1958.
Oṃ Vāgīśvara Mūḥ
This mantra is very popular in {{ill|Nepal|en|Nepal|WD=Q837|lt=Nepal}}, where Vāgīśvara Mañjuśrī is a popular deity. Another Mañjuśrī mantra is the mantra for Mañjuvajra, a tantric form of Mañjuśrī associated with the {{ill|Guhyasamāja Tantra|en|Guhyasamāja Tantra|WD=Q1400398|lt=Guhyasamaja}} tradition, it is:Bhattacharyya, Benoytosh. ''The Indian Buddhist Iconography Mainly Based on the Sādhanamālā and Other Cognate Tāntric Texts of Rituals'' (2nd Ed.)'','' pp. 117. K. L. MUKHOPADHYAY, Calcutta, 1958.
Oṃ Mañjuvajra Hūṃ
==In Buddhist cultures== {{MahayanaBuddhism}} [[File:Yulin Cave 3 w wall Manjusri (Western Xia).jpg|thumb|A painting of the Buddhist ''manjusri'' from the {{ill|Yulin Caves|en|Yulin Caves|WD=Q751622|lt=Yulin Caves}} of {{ill|Gansu|en|Gansu|WD=Q42392|lt=Gansu}}, China, from the {{ill|Tangut people|en|Tangut people|WD=Q756608|lt=Tangut}}-led {{ill|Western Xia|en|Western Xia|WD=Q7427|lt=Western Xia}} dynasty]] ===In China=== Mañjuśrī is known in China as ''Wenshu'' ({{zh|c=文殊|p=Wénshū}}). {{ill|Mount Wutai|en|Mount Wutai|WD=Q120314|lt=Mount Wutai}} in {{ill|Shanxi|en|Shanxi|WD=Q46913|lt=Shanxi}}, one of the four {{ill|Sacred Mountains of China|en|Sacred Mountains of China|WD=Q1062231|lt=Sacred Mountains of China}}, is considered by Chinese Buddhists to be his {{ill|Bodhimaṇḍa|en|Bodhimaṇḍa|WD=Q1939884|lt=Bodhimaṇḍa}}. He was said to bestow spectacular visionary experiences to those on selected mountain peaks and caves there. In Mount Wutai's {{ill|Foguang Temple|en|Foguang Temple|WD=Q44615|lt=Foguang Temple}}, the Manjusri Hall to the right of its main hall was recognized to have been built in 1137 during the {{ill|Jin dynasty (1115–1234)|en|Jin dynasty (1115–1234)|WD=Q5066|lt=Jin dynasty}}. The hall was thoroughly studied, mapped and first photographed by early twentieth-century Chinese architects {{ill|Liang Sicheng|en|Liang Sicheng|WD=Q71874|lt=Liang Sicheng}} and {{ill|Lin Huiyin|en|Lin Huiyin|WD=Q467140|lt=Lin Huiyin}}.Liang, Ssucheng. ''A Pictorial History of Chinese Architecture''. Ed. Wilma Fairbank. Cambridge, Michigan: The MIT Press, 1984. These made it a popular place of pilgrimage, but patriarchs including {{ill|en:Linji Yixuan|en|en:Linji Yixuan|WD=Q326950|lt=en:Linji Yixuan}} and {{ill|Yunmen Wenyan|en|Yunmen Wenyan|WD=Q2165671|lt=Yunmen Wenyan}} declared the mountain off limits.*See Robert M. Gimello, "Chang Shang-ying on Wu-t'ai Shan", in Pilgrims and Sacred Sites in China:, ed. Susan Naquin and Chün-fang Yü (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1992), pp. 89–149; and Steven Heine, "Visions, Divisions, Revisions: The Encounter Between Iconoclasm and Supernaturalism in Kōan Cases about Mount Wu-t'ai", in The Kōan, pp. 137–167. Mount Wutai was also associated with the {{ill|East Mountain Teaching|en|East Mountain Teaching|WD=Q11526728|lt=East Mountain Teaching}}.{{Cite book | last= Heine | first= Steven | title= Opening a Mountain: Koans of the Zen Masters | publisher= Oxford University Press | location= USA | page= [https://archive.org/details/openingmountain00stev/page/ ] | year= 2002 | isbn= 0-19-513586-5 | url-access= registration | url= https://archive.org/details/openingmountain00stev/page/ }} Mañjuśrī has been associated with Mount Wutai since ancient times. Paul Williams writes:Williams, Paul. ''Mahayana Buddhism: The Doctrinal Foundations.'' 2000. p. 227 {{quote|Apparently the association of Mañjuśrī with Wutai (Wu-t'ai) Shan in north China was known in classical times in India itself, identified by Chinese scholars with the mountain in the 'north-east' (when seen from India or {{ill|Central Asia|en|Central Asia|WD=Q27275|lt=Central Asia}}) referred to as the abode of Mañjuśrī in the ''{{ill|Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra|en|Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra|WD=Q790258|lt=Avataṃsaka Sūtra}}''. There are said to have been pilgrimages from India and other Asian countries to Wutai Shan by the seventh century.}} According to official histories from the {{ill|Qing dynasty|en|Qing dynasty|WD=Q8733|lt=Qing dynasty}}, {{ill|Nurhaci|en|Nurhaci|WD=Q311189|lt=Nurhaci}}, a military leader of the {{ill|Jurchen people|en|Jurchen people|WD=Q753880|lt=Jurchens}} of {{ill|Northeast China|en|Northeast China|WD=Q1057925|lt=Northeast China}} and founder of what became the Qing dynasty, named his tribe after Mañjuśrī as the [[:en:Manchus|Manchus]].{{Cite book|last=Agui|title=满洲源流考 (the Origin of Manchus)|publisher=Liaoning Nationality Publishing House|year=1988|isbn=9787805270609|url=http://book.douban.com/subject/4106389/}} The true origin of the name Manchu is disputed.{{Cite book|first=Chongnian|last=Yan|title=明亡清兴六十年 (彩图珍藏版)|publisher=Zhonghua Book Company|year=2008|isbn=9787101059472|url=http://book.douban.com/subject/2359481/}} Monk {{ill|Hanshan (poet)|en|Hanshan (poet)|WD=Q930333|lt=Hanshan}} ({{lang|zh|寒山}}) is widely considered to be a metaphorical manifestation of Mañjuśrī. He is known for having co-written the following famous poem about reincarnation with monk {{ill|Shide (monk)|en|Shide (monk)|WD=Q752964|lt=Shide}}:{{cite web|url=http://foxue.163.com/photonew/B06C0324/114.html|title=诗僧寒山与拾得:文殊菩萨普贤菩萨化身|publisher=NetEase Buddhism Channel|date=2014-12-10|language=zh|location=Beijing}}{{cite web|url=http://www.lingshh.com/wuyuefojiao/hantingjie.htm|title=寒山诗赏析|author=韩廷杰|publisher=灵山海会期刊社|language=zh|location=Zhejiang}} {{poem quote|Drumming your grandpa in the shrine, Cooking your aunts in the pot, Marrying your grandma in the past, Should I laugh or not? {{lang|zh-Hant|堂上打鼓打公皮， 鍋內煎煮是姑娘， 三世祖母娶為婦， 我今不笑等何時。}}}} In {{ill|Tibetan Buddhism|en|Tibetan Buddhism|WD=Q483889|lt=Tibetan Buddhism}}, Mañjuśrī manifests in a number of different {{ill|Tantra|en|Tantra|WD=Q181510|lt=Tantric}} forms. {{ill|Yamantaka|en|Yamantaka|WD=Q1348317|lt=Yamāntaka}} (meaning 'terminator of {{ill|Yama|en|Yama|WD=Q45097|lt=Yama}} i.e. Death') is the [[:en:Wrathful deity|wrathful]] manifestation of Mañjuśrī, popular within the {{ill|Gelug|en|Gelug|WD=Q319218|lt=Gelug}} school of Tibetan Buddhism. Other variations upon his traditional form as Mañjuśrī include {{ill|Mañjuśrīnāmasamgīti|en|Mañjuśrīnāmasamgīti|WD=Q3577095|lt=Namasangiti}}, Arapacana Manjushri, etc. In Tibetan Buddhism, Mañjuśrī is also an ''{{ill|Yidam|en|Yidam|WD=Q2072049|lt=Yidam}}''. The {{ill|Emperor Manjushri|en|Emperor Manjushri|WD=Q11080008|lt=Emperor Manjushri}} as a honorific title was also given to Qing emperors such as the {{ill|Qianlong Emperor|en|Qianlong Emperor|WD=Q19133|lt=Qianlong Emperor}}. In the Taoist pantheon, Mañjuśrī is adopted as a Taoist deity known as {{ill|Wenshu Guangfa Tianzun|en|Wenshu Guangfa Tianzun|WD=Q7982957|lt=Wenshu Guangfa Tianzun}}. This deity appears in the Ming Dynasty novel ''[[:en:Fengshen Yanyi|Fengshen Yanyi]]'' as a senior disciple of {{ill|Yuanshi Tianzun|en|Yuanshi Tianzun|WD=Q1195885|lt=Yuanshi Tianzun}}, the highest deity in Taoism. However, the books ''Qunxian Xianpo Tianmen'' and ''Western Tang Dynasty Biography'' state that Wenshu Guangfa Tianzun and Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva are not the same person.{{cite book |title=四川道敎史话 [Sichuan Taoist History]|date=1985 |publisher=四川人民出版社 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vrwEAQAAIAAJ&q=%E6%96%87%E6%AE%8A%E5%B9%BF%E6%B3%95%E5%A4%A9%E5%B0%8A |quote=... 文殊广法天尊,就是文殊,至于观音,改名叫作慈航道人,自称“贫道乃灵鹫山元觉洞燃灯道人”者,前身就是燃灯佛,西方极乐世界的孔雀明王,成了准提道人。|language=zh}}{{cite book |title=当代 |date=2009 |publisher=人民文学出版社 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iRJMAQAAIAAJ&q=%E6%96%87%E6%AE%8A%E5%B9%BF%E6%B3%95%E5%A4%A9%E5%B0%8A|quote=... 文殊广法天尊” ,这与三教中的大师法号习惯带“子” ,如“广成子” “云中子” “赤精子”也大异其趣。却不可认为这位“文殊”便真是佛家那位“文殊菩萨” [Translation:... Wenshu Guangfa Tianzun," this differs significantly from the usual naming conventions for masters in the Three Religions, where they typically include "Zi" (子) in their titles, such as "Guangcheng Zi," "Yunzhong Zi," "Chijing Zi," and others. However, it should not be assumed that this "Wenshu" is indeed the same as the Buddhist figure "Manjushri Bodhisattva."] |language=zh}} ({{ill|East Java|en|East Java|WD=Q3586|lt=East Java}}, {{ill|Indonesia|en|Indonesia|WD=Q252|lt=Indonesia}}), probably made in 1823 by J.Th. Bik in Batavia.]] ===In Nepal=== According to {{ill|Swayambhu Purana|en|Swayambhu Purana|WD=Q7654077|lt=Swayambhu Purana}}, the {{ill|Kathmandu Valley|en|Kathmandu Valley|WD=Q970717|lt=Kathmandu Valley}} was once a lake. It is believed that Mañjuśrī came on a pilgrimage from his earthly abode-[[:en:Wutaishan|Wutaishan]] (five-peaked mountain) in China. He saw a lotus flower in the center of the lake, which emitted brilliant radiance. He cut a gorge at Chovar with his flaming sword to allow the lake to drain. The place where the lotus flower settled became the great {{ill|Swayambhunath|en|Swayambhunath|WD=Q12946982|lt=Swayambhunath}} Stupa, and the valley thus became habitable. ===In Indonesia=== In eighth century {{ill|Java|en|Java|WD=Q3757|lt=Java}} during the [[:en:Mataram Kingdom|Mataram Kingdom]], Mañjuśrī was a prominent deity revered by the [[:en:Sailendra dynasty|Sailendra dynasty]], patrons of Mahayana Buddhism. The {{ill|Kelurak inscription|en|Kelurak inscription|WD=Q4263126|lt=Kelurak inscription}} (782) and {{ill|Manjusrigrha inscription|en|Manjusrigrha inscription|WD=Q10991107|lt=Manjusrigrha inscription}} (792) mentioned about the construction of a grand Prasada named ''Vajrāsana Mañjuśrīgṛha'' (Vajra House of Mañjuśrī) identified today as {{ill|Sewu|en|Sewu|WD=Q2936254|lt=Sewu}} temple, located just 800 meters north of the {{ill|Prambanan|en|Prambanan|WD=Q47721|lt=Prambanan}}. Sewu is the second largest Buddhist temple in Central Java after {{ill|Borobudur|en|Borobudur|WD=Q42798|lt=Borobudur}}. The depiction of Mañjuśrī in Sailendra art is similar to those of the {{ill|Pala Empire|en|Pala Empire|WD=Q668412|lt=Pala Empire}} style of [[:en:Nalanda|Nalanda]], {{ill|Bihar|en|Bihar|WD=Q1165|lt=Bihar}}. Mañjuśrī was portrayed as a youthful handsome man with the palm of his hands tattooed with the image of a flower. His right hand is facing down with an open palm while his left-hand holds an ''utpala'' (blue lotus). He also uses the necklace made of tiger {{ill|canine tooth|en|canine tooth|WD=Q19625|lt=canine teeth}}. ==Gallery== File:Hermitage hall 342 - 03.jpg|Mañjuśrī figure from [[:en:Candi Jago|Candi Jago]], 14th century Java, Indonesia. File:WLA ima Manjusri.jpg|Mañjuśrī figure brandishing sword of wisdom in {{ill|Nepal|en|Nepal|WD=Q837|lt=Nepal}} File:Astasahasrika Prajnaparamita Manjusri Bodhisattva.jpeg|Palm leaf manuscript painting of Mañjuśrī. [[:en:Nalanda|Nalanda]], {{ill|Bihar|en|Bihar|WD=Q1165|lt=Bihar}}, India. File:COLLECTIE TROPENMUSEUM Zilveren Manjusri beeld afkomstig uit Ngemplak Semongan TMnr 10016132.jpg|Silver figure of Mañjuśrī holding a long-stemmed lotus. Central Java, Indonesia. File:He Chaozong 1.JPG|[[:en:Blanc de Chine|Blanc de Chine]] figure of Mañjuśrī holding a ''{{ill|Ruyi (scepter)|en|Ruyi (scepter)|WD=Q1448880|lt=ruyi}}'' scepter. China, 17th century. File:Manjusri Chua Quan Am.jpg|Mañjuśrī on lion with [[cintamani]]. {{ill|Quan Am Temple|en|Quan Am Temple|WD=Q7268821|lt=Quan Am Temple}}, {{ill|Ho Chi Minh City|en|Ho Chi Minh City|WD=Q1854|lt=Ho Chi Minh City}}. British Museum.jpg|Bodhisattva Manjushri seated in lalitasana, from China, Jin Dynasty, 12th century CE. British Museum. File:Manjusri, God of Wisdom.jpg|Drawing of Mañjuśrī, Bodhisattva of Wisdom File:艋舺龍山寺文殊菩薩寶像 20240804.jpg|Statue of Mañjuśrī at [[:en:Bangka Lungshan Temple|Bangka Lungshan Temple]], {{ill|Taipei|en|Taipei|WD=Q1867|lt=Taipei}} ==See also== * {{ill|Mañjuśrīmitra|en|Mañjuśrīmitra|WD=Q772713|lt=Mañjuśrīmitra}} * {{ill|Manjusri Monastery|en|Manjusri Monastery|WD=Q148612|lt=Manjusri Monastery}} * {{ill|Washing the Elephant|en|Washing the Elephant|WD=Q85814493|lt=Washing the Elephant}} ==References== ===Citations=== {{reflist}} ===Sources=== * {{citation |editor-last=Doniger |editor-first=Wendy |editor-link=Wendy Doniger |title=Purana Perennis: Reciprocity and Transformation in Hindu and Jaina Texts |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-kZFzHCuiFAC |year=1993 |publisher=[[State University of New York Press]] |isbn=0-7914-1381-0 }} ==Further reading== Harrison, Paul M. (2000). [https://web.archive.org/web/20120525221148/http://www.chibs.edu.tw/ch_html/chbj/13/chbj1335.htm Mañjuśrī and the Cult of the Celestial Bodhisattvas], Chung-Hwa Buddhist Journal 13, 157-193 ==External links== {{Commons Category:kk]] [[Category|Manjusri}} *[http://www.khandro.net/deity_manjushri.htm Manjushri at Khandro Net.] *[http://themathesontrust.org/library/manjusri-mantra Page dedicated to the Manjusri mantra, with several audio versions.] {{Buddhism topics}} {{Bodhisattvas}} {{Chinese Buddhist Pantheon}} [[wikt:%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%9E%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%9C%E0%A5%81|mañju]] [[file:Center detail, from- Interior of a Book Cover- Manjuvajra Embracing His Consort, with Attendant Lamas MET DP335604 (cropped).jpg|thumb|Mañjuvajra, a tantric form of Mañjuśrī]] [[file:KITLV A314 - Zwart-wit krijttekening vermoedelijk in 1823 door J.Th. Diệu Âm | tagalog_name = Mangushli | cebuano_name = Mangushli | veneration = {{ill|Mahayana|en|Mahayana|WD=Q48362|lt=Mahayana}}, {{ill|Vajrayana|en|Vajrayana|WD=Q172175|lt=Vajrayana}} | attributes = | shakti = | preceded_by = | succeeded_by = }} '''Manjushri''' ({{langx|sa|मञ्जुश्री|Mañjuśrī}}) is a ''{{ill|Bodhisattva|en|Bodhisattva|WD=Q178149|lt=Bodhisattva}}'' who represents ''{{ill|Prajñā (Buddhism)|en|Prajñā (Buddhism)|WD=Q849649|lt=prajñā}}'' (transcendent wisdom) of the Buddhas in [[:en:Mahāyāna Buddhism|Mahāyāna Buddhism]]. The name "Mañjuśrī" is a combination of Sanskrit word "" and an honorific "[[:en:śrī|śrī]]"; it can be literally translated as "Beautiful One with Glory" or "Beautiful One with Auspiciousness". Mañjuśrī is also known by the fuller name of Mañjuśrīkumārabhūta ({{lang|sa|मञ्जुश्रीकुमारभूत}}),Keown, Damien (editor) with Hodge, Stephen; Jones, Charles; Tinti, Paola (2003). ''A Dictionary of Buddhism.'' Oxford, UK: Oxford University Press. {{ISBN|0-19-860560-9}} p.172. literally "Mañjuśrī, Still a Youth" or, less literally, "Prince Mañjuśrī". Another name of Mañjuśrī is Mañjughoṣa. ==In Mahāyāna Buddhism== [[File:Manjushri statue. Lalung Gompa, Spiti.jpg|thumb|left|200px|Manjushri statue, Lhalung Gompa, [[:en:Spiti Valley|Spiti Valley]], India]] [[File:Manjushri at Buddha Tooth Relic Temple and Museum.JPG|thumb|200px|Manjushri, seated on a blue lion at {{ill|Buddha Tooth Relic Temple and Museum|en|Buddha Tooth Relic Temple and Museum|WD=Q839965|lt=Buddha Tooth Relic Temple and Museum}}, {{ill|Singapore|en|Singapore|WD=Q334|lt=Singapore}}.]] [[File:The Bodhisattva Monju (Manjushri), Kamakura period, Japan.jpg|thumb|200px|Bodhisattva Monju (Manjushri), {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period}}, {{ill|Tokyo National Museum|en|Tokyo National Museum|WD=Q653433|lt=Tokyo National Museum}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan}}]] Scholars have identified Mañjuśrī as the oldest and most significant bodhisattva in Mahāyāna literature.A View of Manjushri: Wisdom and Its Crown Prince in Pala Period India. Harrington, Laura. Doctoral Thesis, Columbia University, 2002 Mañjuśrī is first referred to in early [[:en:Mahāyāna sūtras|Mahāyāna sūtras]] such as the [[:en:Prajñāpāramitā|Prajñāpāramitā]] ''sūtra''s and through this association, very early in the tradition he came to symbolize the embodiment of ''prajñā'' (transcendent wisdom). The ''{{ill|en:Lotus Sutra|en|en:Lotus Sutra|WD=Q861212|lt=en:Lotus Sutra}}'' assigns him a [[:en:Pure land|Pure land]] called ''Vimala'', which according to the ''{{ill|Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra|en|Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra|WD=Q790258|lt=Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra}}'' is located in the East. His pure land is predicted to be one of the two best pure lands in all of existence in all the past, present, and future. When he attains {{ill|Buddhahood|en|Buddhahood|WD=Q56247062|lt=Buddhahood}} his name will be Universal Sight{{Citation needed|date=September 2022}}. In the ''Lotus Sūtra'', Mañjuśrī also leads the {{ill|en:Longnü|en|en:Longnü|WD=Q6674175|lt=Nagaraja's daughter}} to enlightenment. He also figures in the ''[[:en:Vimalakīrti Sūtra|Vimalakīrti Sūtra]]'' in a debate with [[:en:Vimalakīrti|Vimalakīrti]] where he is presented as a Bodhisattva who discusses non-duality with him. An example of a wisdom teaching of Mañjuśrī can be found in the ''Saptaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra'' ({{ill|Taishō Tripiṭaka|en|Taishō Tripiṭaka|WD=Q837315|lt=Taishō Tripiṭaka}} 232).{{citation|url=http://www.acmuller.net/descriptive_catalogue/files/k0010.html|title=The Korean Buddhist Canon: A Descriptive Catalog (T 232)}} This ''sūtra'' contains a dialogue between Mañjuśrī and the Buddha on the One [[:en:Samādhi|Samādhi]] (Skt. ''Ekavyūha Samādhi''). {{ill|Sheng-yen|en|Sheng-yen|WD=Q712896|lt=Sheng-yen}} renders the following teaching of Mañjuśrī, for entering ''samādhi'' naturally through transcendent wisdom: {{quote|Contemplate the five {{ill|Skandha|en|Skandha|WD=Q747858|lt=Skandha}}s as originally empty and quiescent, non-arising, non-perishing, equal, without differentiation. Constantly thus practicing, day or night, whether sitting, walking, standing or lying down, finally one reaches an inconceivable state without any obstruction or form. This is the Samadhi of One Act ({{zh|c=一行三昧|p=Yīxíng sānmèi|labels=no}}).Sheng-Yen, Master (聖嚴法師)(1988). [https://web.archive.org/web/20121011012531/http://ccbs.ntu.edu.tw/FULLTEXT/JR-BJ001/02_10.htm ''Tso-Ch'an''], p.364}} ==Vajrayāna Buddhism== Within [[:en:Vajrayāna|Vajrayāna]] Buddhism, Mañjuśrī is a meditational deity and considered a fully enlightened Buddha. In {{ill|Shingon Buddhism|en|Shingon Buddhism|WD=Q550182|lt=Shingon Buddhism}}, he is one of the {{ill|Thirteen Buddhas|en|Thirteen Buddhas|WD=Q3538361|lt=Thirteen Buddhas}} to whom disciples devote themselves. He figures extensively in many esoteric texts such as the ''[[:en:Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa|Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa]]'' and the ''{{ill|Mañjuśrīnāmasamgīti|en|Mañjuśrīnāmasamgīti|WD=Q3577095|lt=Mañjuśrīnāmasamgīti}}''. His consort in some traditions is [[Saraswati]]. The ''Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa'', which later came to be classified under [[Outer Tantras#Kriyatantra|Kriyātantra]], states that ''mantra''s taught in the [[:en:Śaiva|Śaiva]], Garuḍa, and [[:en:Vaiṣṇava|Vaiṣṇava]] ''tantra''s will be effective if applied by Buddhists since they were all taught originally by Mañjuśrī.Sanderson, Alexis. "The Śaiva Age: The Rise and Dominance of Śaivism during the Early Medieval Period." In: Genesis and Development of Tantrism, edited by Shingo Einoo. Tokyo: Institute of Oriental Culture, University of Tokyo, 2009. Institute of Oriental Culture Special Series, 23, pp. 129-131. ==Iconography== Mañjuśrī is depicted as a male bodhisattva wielding a flaming sword in his right hand, representing the realization of transcendent wisdom which cuts down ignorance and duality. The scripture supported by the [[:en:Padma (attribute)|padma]] (lotus) held in his left hand is a ''Prajñāpāramitā sūtra'', representing his attainment of ultimate realization from the blossoming of wisdom. Mañjuśrī is often depicted as riding or seated on a blue {{ill|Lion|en|Lion|WD=Q140|lt=Lion}}, as can be seen at {{ill|Buddha Tooth Relic Temple and Museum|en|Buddha Tooth Relic Temple and Museum|WD=Q839965|lt=Buddha Tooth Relic Temple and Museum}} in {{ill|Singapore|en|Singapore|WD=Q334|lt=Singapore}}. (see opposite), or sitting on the skin of a lion. This represents the use of wisdom to tame the mind, which is compared to riding or subduing a ferocious lion. In Chinese and Japanese Buddhist art, Mañjuśrī's sword is sometimes replaced with a ''{{ill|Ruyi (scepter)|en|Ruyi (scepter)|WD=Q1448880|lt=ruyi}}'' scepter, especially in representations of his ''{{ill|Vimalakirti Sutra|en|Vimalakirti Sutra|WD=Q110646|lt=Vimalakirti Sutra}}'' discussion with the layman {{ill|Vimalakirti|en|Vimalakirti|WD=Q2502143|lt=Vimalakirti}}.Davidson, J. LeRoy, "The Origin and Early Use of the Ju-i", ''Artibus Asiae'' 1950,13.4, 240. According to {{ill|Berthold Laufer|en|Berthold Laufer|WD=Q71600|lt=Berthold Laufer}}, the first Chinese representation of a ''ruyi'' was in an 8th-century Mañjuśrī painting by {{ill|Wu Daozi|en|Wu Daozi|WD=Q1196022|lt=Wu Daozi}}, showing it held in his right hand taking the place of the usual sword. In subsequent Chinese and Japanese paintings of Buddhas, a ''ruyi'' was occasionally represented as a Padma with a long stem curved like a ''ruyi''.Laufer, Berthold, ''[https://openlibrary.org/books/OL7181158M/Jade Jade, a Study in Chinese Archaeology and Religion]'', Field Museum of Natural History, 1912, 339. He is one of the Four Great Bodhisattvas of {{ill|Chinese Buddhism|en|Chinese Buddhism|WD=Q847618|lt=Chinese Buddhism}}, the other three being {{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|Kṣitigarbha|WD=Q604687|lt=Kṣitigarbha}}, {{ill|Avalokiteśvara|en|Avalokiteśvara|WD=Q193849|lt=Avalokiteśvara}}, and {{ill|Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|en|Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|WD=Q868306|lt=Samantabhadra}}. In China, he is often paired with Samantabhadra{{Citation needed|date=September 2022}}. In {{ill|Tibetan Buddhism|en|Tibetan Buddhism|WD=Q483889|lt=Tibetan Buddhism}}, Mañjuśrī is sometimes depicted in a trinity with Avalokiteśvara and [[:en:Vajrapāṇi|Vajrapāṇi]]{{Citation needed|date=September 2022}}. ==Mantras== === Arapacana mantra === A {{ill|Mantra|en|Mantra|WD=Q131510|lt=Mantra}} commonly associated with Mañjuśrī is the following:Buswell, Robert. Lopez, Donald. ''The Princeton Dictionary of Buddhism.'' 2013. p. 527 :''oṃ arapacana dhīḥ'' The Arapacana is a {{ill|Syllabary|en|Syllabary|WD=Q182133|lt=Syllabary}} consisting of forty-two letters, and is named after the first five letters: ''a, ra, pa, ca, na''.Buswell, Robert. Lopez, Donald. ''The Princeton Dictionary of Buddhism.'' 2013. p. 61 This syllabary was most widely used for the [[:en:Gāndhārī language|Gāndhārī language]] with the {{ill|Kharosthi|en|Kharosthi|WD=Q1161266|lt=Kharoṣṭhī script}} but also appears in some Sanskrit texts. The syllabary features in Mahāyāna texts such as the longer ''[[:en:Prajñāpāramitā|Prajñāpāramitā]]'' texts, the ''[[:en:Gaṇḍavyūha Sūtra|Gaṇḍavyūha Sūtra]]'', the ''{{ill|Lalitavistara Sūtra|en|Lalitavistara Sūtra|WD=Q1381826|lt=Lalitavistara Sūtra}}'', the ''[[:en:Avataṃsaka Sūtra|Avataṃsaka Sūtra]]'', the ''{{ill|Dharmaguptaka|en|Dharmaguptaka|WD=Q2445824|lt=Dharmaguptaka}} {{ill|Vinaya|en|Vinaya|WD=Q848764|lt=Vinaya}}'', and the ''[[:en:Mūlasarvāstivāda|Mūlasarvāstivāda]] Vinaya''. In some of these texts, the Arapacana syllabary serves as a {{ill|Mnemonic|en|Mnemonic|WD=Q191062|lt=Mnemonic}} for important Mahāyāna concepts. Due to its association with him, ''Arapacana'' may even serve as an alternate name for Mañjuśrī. The ''Sutra on Perfect Wisdom'' (Conze 1975) defines the significance of each syllable thus: # ''A'' is a door to the insight that all dharmas are unproduced from the very beginning (''ādya-anutpannatvād''). # ''RA'' is a door to the insight that all dharmas are without dirt (''rajas''). # ''PA'' is a door to the insight that all dharmas have been expounded in the ultimate sense (''paramārtha''). # ''CA'' is a door to the insight that the decrease (''cyavana'') or rebirth of any dharma cannot be apprehended, because all dharmas do not decrease, nor are they reborn. # ''NA'' is a door to the insight that the names (i.e. ''nāma'') of all dharmas have vanished; the essential nature behind names cannot be gained or lost. Tibetan pronunciation is slightly different and so the Tibetan characters read: ''{{IAST|oṃ a ra pa tsa na dhīḥ}}'' ({{bo|w=om a ra pa tsa na d+hIH|t=ༀ་ཨ་ར་པ་ཙ་ན་དྷཱི༔|lang=yes}}).[http://www.visiblemantra.org/manjusri.html] - Visible Mantra's website In Tibetan tradition, this mantra is believed to enhance wisdom and improve one's skills in debating, memory, writing, and other literary abilities. "{{IAST|Dhīḥ}}" is the seed syllable of the mantra and is chanted with greater emphasis and also repeated a number of times as a [[:en:decrescendo|decrescendo]]. === Other mantras === According to the {{ill|Mañjuśrī-mūla-kalpa|en|Mañjuśrī-mūla-kalpa|WD=Q6799169|lt=''Mañjuśrī­mūlakalpa''}}, "the ultimate heart essence of Mañjuśrī, which accomplishes all endeavors" is the following mantra:{{Cite web |title=The Root Manual of the Rites of Mañjuśrī / 84000 Reading Room |url=https://read.84000.co/translation/toh543.html |access-date=2024-03-22 |website=84000 Translating The Words of The Buddha |language=en}}
Namaḥ sarvabuddhānām oṁ maṁ
The ''Sādhanamālā'' also contains a popular mantra which refers to Mañjuśrī as the "lord of speech" (Vāgīśvara):Bhattacharyya, Benoytosh. ''The Indian Buddhist Iconography Mainly Based on the Sādhanamālā and Other Cognate Tāntric Texts of Rituals'' (2nd Ed.)'','' pp. 113, 116. K. L. MUKHOPADHYAY, Calcutta, 1958.
Oṃ Vāgīśvara Mūḥ
This mantra is very popular in {{ill|Nepal|en|Nepal|WD=Q837|lt=Nepal}}, where Vāgīśvara Mañjuśrī is a popular deity. Another Mañjuśrī mantra is the mantra for Mañjuvajra, a tantric form of Mañjuśrī associated with the {{ill|Guhyasamāja Tantra|en|Guhyasamāja Tantra|WD=Q1400398|lt=Guhyasamaja}} tradition, it is:Bhattacharyya, Benoytosh. ''The Indian Buddhist Iconography Mainly Based on the Sādhanamālā and Other Cognate Tāntric Texts of Rituals'' (2nd Ed.)'','' pp. 117. K. L. MUKHOPADHYAY, Calcutta, 1958.
Oṃ Mañjuvajra Hūṃ
==In Buddhist cultures== {{MahayanaBuddhism}} [[File:Yulin Cave 3 w wall Manjusri (Western Xia).jpg|thumb|A painting of the Buddhist ''manjusri'' from the {{ill|Yulin Caves|en|Yulin Caves|WD=Q751622|lt=Yulin Caves}} of {{ill|Gansu|en|Gansu|WD=Q42392|lt=Gansu}}, China, from the {{ill|Tangut people|en|Tangut people|WD=Q756608|lt=Tangut}}-led {{ill|Western Xia|en|Western Xia|WD=Q7427|lt=Western Xia}} dynasty]] ===In China=== Mañjuśrī is known in China as ''Wenshu'' ({{zh|c=文殊|p=Wénshū}}). {{ill|Mount Wutai|en|Mount Wutai|WD=Q120314|lt=Mount Wutai}} in {{ill|Shanxi|en|Shanxi|WD=Q46913|lt=Shanxi}}, one of the four {{ill|Sacred Mountains of China|en|Sacred Mountains of China|WD=Q1062231|lt=Sacred Mountains of China}}, is considered by Chinese Buddhists to be his {{ill|Bodhimaṇḍa|en|Bodhimaṇḍa|WD=Q1939884|lt=Bodhimaṇḍa}}. He was said to bestow spectacular visionary experiences to those on selected mountain peaks and caves there. In Mount Wutai's {{ill|Foguang Temple|en|Foguang Temple|WD=Q44615|lt=Foguang Temple}}, the Manjusri Hall to the right of its main hall was recognized to have been built in 1137 during the {{ill|Jin dynasty (1115–1234)|en|Jin dynasty (1115–1234)|WD=Q5066|lt=Jin dynasty}}. The hall was thoroughly studied, mapped and first photographed by early twentieth-century Chinese architects {{ill|Liang Sicheng|en|Liang Sicheng|WD=Q71874|lt=Liang Sicheng}} and {{ill|Lin Huiyin|en|Lin Huiyin|WD=Q467140|lt=Lin Huiyin}}.Liang, Ssucheng. ''A Pictorial History of Chinese Architecture''. Ed. Wilma Fairbank. Cambridge, Michigan: The MIT Press, 1984. These made it a popular place of pilgrimage, but patriarchs including {{ill|en:Linji Yixuan|en|en:Linji Yixuan|WD=Q326950|lt=en:Linji Yixuan}} and {{ill|Yunmen Wenyan|en|Yunmen Wenyan|WD=Q2165671|lt=Yunmen Wenyan}} declared the mountain off limits.*See Robert M. Gimello, "Chang Shang-ying on Wu-t'ai Shan", in Pilgrims and Sacred Sites in China:, ed. Susan Naquin and Chün-fang Yü (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1992), pp. 89–149; and Steven Heine, "Visions, Divisions, Revisions: The Encounter Between Iconoclasm and Supernaturalism in Kōan Cases about Mount Wu-t'ai", in The Kōan, pp. 137–167. Mount Wutai was also associated with the {{ill|East Mountain Teaching|en|East Mountain Teaching|WD=Q11526728|lt=East Mountain Teaching}}.{{Cite book | last= Heine | first= Steven | title= Opening a Mountain: Koans of the Zen Masters | publisher= Oxford University Press | location= USA | page= [https://archive.org/details/openingmountain00stev/page/ ] | year= 2002 | isbn= 0-19-513586-5 | url-access= registration | url= https://archive.org/details/openingmountain00stev/page/ }} Mañjuśrī has been associated with Mount Wutai since ancient times. Paul Williams writes:Williams, Paul. ''Mahayana Buddhism: The Doctrinal Foundations.'' 2000. p. 227 {{quote|Apparently the association of Mañjuśrī with Wutai (Wu-t'ai) Shan in north China was known in classical times in India itself, identified by Chinese scholars with the mountain in the 'north-east' (when seen from India or {{ill|Central Asia|en|Central Asia|WD=Q27275|lt=Central Asia}}) referred to as the abode of Mañjuśrī in the ''{{ill|Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra|en|Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra|WD=Q790258|lt=Avataṃsaka Sūtra}}''. There are said to have been pilgrimages from India and other Asian countries to Wutai Shan by the seventh century.}} According to official histories from the {{ill|Qing dynasty|en|Qing dynasty|WD=Q8733|lt=Qing dynasty}}, {{ill|Nurhaci|en|Nurhaci|WD=Q311189|lt=Nurhaci}}, a military leader of the {{ill|Jurchen people|en|Jurchen people|WD=Q753880|lt=Jurchens}} of {{ill|Northeast China|en|Northeast China|WD=Q1057925|lt=Northeast China}} and founder of what became the Qing dynasty, named his tribe after Mañjuśrī as the [[:en:Manchus|Manchus]].{{Cite book|last=Agui|title=满洲源流考 (the Origin of Manchus)|publisher=Liaoning Nationality Publishing House|year=1988|isbn=9787805270609|url=http://book.douban.com/subject/4106389/}} The true origin of the name Manchu is disputed.{{Cite book|first=Chongnian|last=Yan|title=明亡清兴六十年 (彩图珍藏版)|publisher=Zhonghua Book Company|year=2008|isbn=9787101059472|url=http://book.douban.com/subject/2359481/}} Monk {{ill|Hanshan (poet)|en|Hanshan (poet)|WD=Q930333|lt=Hanshan}} ({{lang|zh|寒山}}) is widely considered to be a metaphorical manifestation of Mañjuśrī. He is known for having co-written the following famous poem about reincarnation with monk {{ill|Shide (monk)|en|Shide (monk)|WD=Q752964|lt=Shide}}:{{cite web|url=http://foxue.163.com/photonew/B06C0324/114.html|title=诗僧寒山与拾得:文殊菩萨普贤菩萨化身|publisher=NetEase Buddhism Channel|date=2014-12-10|language=zh|location=Beijing}}{{cite web|url=http://www.lingshh.com/wuyuefojiao/hantingjie.htm|title=寒山诗赏析|author=韩廷杰|publisher=灵山海会期刊社|language=zh|location=Zhejiang}} {{poem quote|Drumming your grandpa in the shrine, Cooking your aunts in the pot, Marrying your grandma in the past, Should I laugh or not? {{lang|zh-Hant|堂上打鼓打公皮， 鍋內煎煮是姑娘， 三世祖母娶為婦， 我今不笑等何時。}}}} In {{ill|Tibetan Buddhism|en|Tibetan Buddhism|WD=Q483889|lt=Tibetan Buddhism}}, Mañjuśrī manifests in a number of different {{ill|Tantra|en|Tantra|WD=Q181510|lt=Tantric}} forms. {{ill|Yamantaka|en|Yamantaka|WD=Q1348317|lt=Yamāntaka}} (meaning 'terminator of {{ill|Yama|en|Yama|WD=Q45097|lt=Yama}} i.e. Death') is the [[:en:Wrathful deity|wrathful]] manifestation of Mañjuśrī, popular within the {{ill|Gelug|en|Gelug|WD=Q319218|lt=Gelug}} school of Tibetan Buddhism. Other variations upon his traditional form as Mañjuśrī include {{ill|Mañjuśrīnāmasamgīti|en|Mañjuśrīnāmasamgīti|WD=Q3577095|lt=Namasangiti}}, Arapacana Manjushri, etc. In Tibetan Buddhism, Mañjuśrī is also an ''{{ill|Yidam|en|Yidam|WD=Q2072049|lt=Yidam}}''. The {{ill|Emperor Manjushri|en|Emperor Manjushri|WD=Q11080008|lt=Emperor Manjushri}} as a honorific title was also given to Qing emperors such as the {{ill|Qianlong Emperor|en|Qianlong Emperor|WD=Q19133|lt=Qianlong Emperor}}. In the Taoist pantheon, Mañjuśrī is adopted as a Taoist deity known as {{ill|Wenshu Guangfa Tianzun|en|Wenshu Guangfa Tianzun|WD=Q7982957|lt=Wenshu Guangfa Tianzun}}. This deity appears in the Ming Dynasty novel ''[[:en:Fengshen Yanyi|Fengshen Yanyi]]'' as a senior disciple of {{ill|Yuanshi Tianzun|en|Yuanshi Tianzun|WD=Q1195885|lt=Yuanshi Tianzun}}, the highest deity in Taoism. However, the books ''Qunxian Xianpo Tianmen'' and ''Western Tang Dynasty Biography'' state that Wenshu Guangfa Tianzun and Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva are not the same person.{{cite book |title=四川道敎史话 [Sichuan Taoist History]|date=1985 |publisher=四川人民出版社 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vrwEAQAAIAAJ&q=%E6%96%87%E6%AE%8A%E5%B9%BF%E6%B3%95%E5%A4%A9%E5%B0%8A |quote=... 文殊广法天尊,就是文殊,至于观音,改名叫作慈航道人,自称“贫道乃灵鹫山元觉洞燃灯道人”者,前身就是燃灯佛,西方极乐世界的孔雀明王,成了准提道人。|language=zh}}{{cite book |title=当代 |date=2009 |publisher=人民文学出版社 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iRJMAQAAIAAJ&q=%E6%96%87%E6%AE%8A%E5%B9%BF%E6%B3%95%E5%A4%A9%E5%B0%8A|quote=... 文殊广法天尊” ,这与三教中的大师法号习惯带“子” ,如“广成子” “云中子” “赤精子”也大异其趣。却不可认为这位“文殊”便真是佛家那位“文殊菩萨” [Translation:... Wenshu Guangfa Tianzun," this differs significantly from the usual naming conventions for masters in the Three Religions, where they typically include "Zi" (子) in their titles, such as "Guangcheng Zi," "Yunzhong Zi," "Chijing Zi," and others. However, it should not be assumed that this "Wenshu" is indeed the same as the Buddhist figure "Manjushri Bodhisattva."] |language=zh}} ({{ill|East Java|en|East Java|WD=Q3586|lt=East Java}}, {{ill|Indonesia|en|Indonesia|WD=Q252|lt=Indonesia}}), probably made in 1823 by J.Th. Bik in Batavia.]] ===In Nepal=== According to {{ill|Swayambhu Purana|en|Swayambhu Purana|WD=Q7654077|lt=Swayambhu Purana}}, the {{ill|Kathmandu Valley|en|Kathmandu Valley|WD=Q970717|lt=Kathmandu Valley}} was once a lake. It is believed that Mañjuśrī came on a pilgrimage from his earthly abode-[[:en:Wutaishan|Wutaishan]] (five-peaked mountain) in China. He saw a lotus flower in the center of the lake, which emitted brilliant radiance. He cut a gorge at Chovar with his flaming sword to allow the lake to drain. The place where the lotus flower settled became the great {{ill|Swayambhunath|en|Swayambhunath|WD=Q12946982|lt=Swayambhunath}} Stupa, and the valley thus became habitable. ===In Indonesia=== In eighth century {{ill|Java|en|Java|WD=Q3757|lt=Java}} during the [[:en:Mataram Kingdom|Mataram Kingdom]], Mañjuśrī was a prominent deity revered by the [[:en:Sailendra dynasty|Sailendra dynasty]], patrons of Mahayana Buddhism. The {{ill|Kelurak inscription|en|Kelurak inscription|WD=Q4263126|lt=Kelurak inscription}} (782) and {{ill|Manjusrigrha inscription|en|Manjusrigrha inscription|WD=Q10991107|lt=Manjusrigrha inscription}} (792) mentioned about the construction of a grand Prasada named ''Vajrāsana Mañjuśrīgṛha'' (Vajra House of Mañjuśrī) identified today as {{ill|Sewu|en|Sewu|WD=Q2936254|lt=Sewu}} temple, located just 800 meters north of the {{ill|Prambanan|en|Prambanan|WD=Q47721|lt=Prambanan}}. Sewu is the second largest Buddhist temple in Central Java after {{ill|Borobudur|en|Borobudur|WD=Q42798|lt=Borobudur}}. The depiction of Mañjuśrī in Sailendra art is similar to those of the {{ill|Pala Empire|en|Pala Empire|WD=Q668412|lt=Pala Empire}} style of [[:en:Nalanda|Nalanda]], {{ill|Bihar|en|Bihar|WD=Q1165|lt=Bihar}}. Mañjuśrī was portrayed as a youthful handsome man with the palm of his hands tattooed with the image of a flower. His right hand is facing down with an open palm while his left-hand holds an ''utpala'' (blue lotus). He also uses the necklace made of tiger {{ill|canine tooth|en|canine tooth|WD=Q19625|lt=canine teeth}}. ==Gallery== File:Hermitage hall 342 - 03.jpg|Mañjuśrī figure from [[:en:Candi Jago|Candi Jago]], 14th century Java, Indonesia. File:WLA ima Manjusri.jpg|Mañjuśrī figure brandishing sword of wisdom in {{ill|Nepal|en|Nepal|WD=Q837|lt=Nepal}} File:Astasahasrika Prajnaparamita Manjusri Bodhisattva.jpeg|Palm leaf manuscript painting of Mañjuśrī. [[:en:Nalanda|Nalanda]], {{ill|Bihar|en|Bihar|WD=Q1165|lt=Bihar}}, India. File:COLLECTIE TROPENMUSEUM Zilveren Manjusri beeld afkomstig uit Ngemplak Semongan TMnr 10016132.jpg|Silver figure of Mañjuśrī holding a long-stemmed lotus. Central Java, Indonesia. File:He Chaozong 1.JPG|[[:en:Blanc de Chine|Blanc de Chine]] figure of Mañjuśrī holding a ''{{ill|Ruyi (scepter)|en|Ruyi (scepter)|WD=Q1448880|lt=ruyi}}'' scepter. China, 17th century. File:Manjusri Chua Quan Am.jpg|Mañjuśrī on lion with [[cintamani]]. {{ill|Quan Am Temple|en|Quan Am Temple|WD=Q7268821|lt=Quan Am Temple}}, {{ill|Ho Chi Minh City|en|Ho Chi Minh City|WD=Q1854|lt=Ho Chi Minh City}}. British Museum.jpg|Bodhisattva Manjushri seated in lalitasana, from China, Jin Dynasty, 12th century CE. British Museum. File:Manjusri, God of Wisdom.jpg|Drawing of Mañjuśrī, Bodhisattva of Wisdom File:艋舺龍山寺文殊菩薩寶像 20240804.jpg|Statue of Mañjuśrī at [[:en:Bangka Lungshan Temple|Bangka Lungshan Temple]], {{ill|Taipei|en|Taipei|WD=Q1867|lt=Taipei}} ==See also== * {{ill|Mañjuśrīmitra|en|Mañjuśrīmitra|WD=Q772713|lt=Mañjuśrīmitra}} * {{ill|Manjusri Monastery|en|Manjusri Monastery|WD=Q148612|lt=Manjusri Monastery}} * {{ill|Washing the Elephant|en|Washing the Elephant|WD=Q85814493|lt=Washing the Elephant}} ==References== ===Citations=== {{reflist}} ===Sources=== * {{citation |editor-last=Doniger |editor-first=Wendy |editor-link=Wendy Doniger |title=Purana Perennis: Reciprocity and Transformation in Hindu and Jaina Texts |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-kZFzHCuiFAC |year=1993 |publisher=[[State University of New York Press]] |isbn=0-7914-1381-0 }} ==Further reading== Harrison, Paul M. (2000). [https://web.archive.org/web/20120525221148/http://www.chibs.edu.tw/ch_html/chbj/13/chbj1335.htm Mañjuśrī and the Cult of the Celestial Bodhisattvas], Chung-Hwa Buddhist Journal 13, 157-193 ==External links== {{Commons Category:kk]] [[Category|Manjusri}} *[http://www.khandro.net/deity_manjushri.htm Manjushri at Khandro Net.] *[http://themathesontrust.org/library/manjusri-mantra Page dedicated to the Manjusri mantra, with several audio versions.] {{Buddhism topics}} {{Bodhisattvas}} {{Chinese Buddhist Pantheon}} [[wikt:%E0%A4%AE%E0%A4%9E%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%9C%E0%A5%81|mañju]] [[file:Center detail, from- Interior of a Book Cover- Manjuvajra Embracing His Consort, with Attendant Lamas MET DP335604 (cropped).jpg|thumb|Mañjuvajra, a tantric form of Mañjuśrī]] [[file:KITLV A314 - Zwart-wit krijttekening vermoedelijk in 1823 door J.Th. Diệu Âm | tagalog_name = Mangushli | cebuano_name = Mangushli | veneration = {{ill|Mahayana|en|Mahayana|WD=Q48362|lt=Mahayana}}, {{ill|Vajrayana|en|Vajrayana|WD=Q172175|lt=Vajrayana}} | attributes = | shakti = | preceded_by = | succeeded_by = }} '''Manjushri''' ({{langx|sa|मञ्जुश्री|Mañjuśrī}}) is a ''{{ill|Bodhisattva|en|Bodhisattva|WD=Q178149|lt=Bodhisattva}}'' who represents ''{{ill|Prajñā (Buddhism)|en|Prajñā (Buddhism)|WD=Q849649|lt=prajñā}}'' (transcendent wisdom) of the Buddhas in [[:en:Mahāyāna Buddhism|Mahāyāna Buddhism]]. The name "Mañjuśrī" is a combination of Sanskrit word "" and an honorific "[[:en:śrī|śrī]]"; it can be literally translated as "Beautiful One with Glory" or "Beautiful One with Auspiciousness". Mañjuśrī is also known by the fuller name of Mañjuśrīkumārabhūta ({{lang|sa|मञ्जुश्रीकुमारभूत}}),Keown, Damien (editor) with Hodge, Stephen; Jones, Charles; Tinti, Paola (2003). ''A Dictionary of Buddhism.'' Oxford, UK: Oxford University Press. {{ISBN|0-19-860560-9}} p.172. literally "Mañjuśrī, Still a Youth" or, less literally, "Prince Mañjuśrī". Another name of Mañjuśrī is Mañjughoṣa. ==In Mahāyāna Buddhism== [[File:Manjushri statue. Lalung Gompa, Spiti.jpg|thumb|left|200px|Manjushri statue, Lhalung Gompa, [[:en:Spiti Valley|Spiti Valley]], India]] [[File:Manjushri at Buddha Tooth Relic Temple and Museum.JPG|thumb|200px|Manjushri, seated on a blue lion at {{ill|Buddha Tooth Relic Temple and Museum|en|Buddha Tooth Relic Temple and Museum|WD=Q839965|lt=Buddha Tooth Relic Temple and Museum}}, {{ill|Singapore|en|Singapore|WD=Q334|lt=Singapore}}.]] [[File:The Bodhisattva Monju (Manjushri), Kamakura period, Japan.jpg|thumb|200px|Bodhisattva Monju (Manjushri), {{ill|Kamakura period|en|Kamakura period|WD=Q236205|lt=Kamakura period}}, {{ill|Tokyo National Museum|en|Tokyo National Museum|WD=Q653433|lt=Tokyo National Museum}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|WD=Q17|lt=Japan}}]] Scholars have identified Mañjuśrī as the oldest and most significant bodhisattva in Mahāyāna literature.A View of Manjushri: Wisdom and Its Crown Prince in Pala Period India. Harrington, Laura. Doctoral Thesis, Columbia University, 2002 Mañjuśrī is first referred to in early [[:en:Mahāyāna sūtras|Mahāyāna sūtras]] such as the [[:en:Prajñāpāramitā|Prajñāpāramitā]] ''sūtra''s and through this association, very early in the tradition he came to symbolize the embodiment of ''prajñā'' (transcendent wisdom). The ''{{ill|en:Lotus Sutra|en|en:Lotus Sutra|WD=Q861212|lt=en:Lotus Sutra}}'' assigns him a [[:en:Pure land|Pure land]] called ''Vimala'', which according to the ''{{ill|Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra|en|Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra|WD=Q790258|lt=Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra}}'' is located in the East. His pure land is predicted to be one of the two best pure lands in all of existence in all the past, present, and future. When he attains {{ill|Buddhahood|en|Buddhahood|WD=Q56247062|lt=Buddhahood}} his name will be Universal Sight{{Citation needed|date=September 2022}}. In the ''Lotus Sūtra'', Mañjuśrī also leads the {{ill|en:Longnü|en|en:Longnü|WD=Q6674175|lt=Nagaraja's daughter}} to enlightenment. He also figures in the ''[[:en:Vimalakīrti Sūtra|Vimalakīrti Sūtra]]'' in a debate with [[:en:Vimalakīrti|Vimalakīrti]] where he is presented as a Bodhisattva who discusses non-duality with him. An example of a wisdom teaching of Mañjuśrī can be found in the ''Saptaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra'' ({{ill|Taishō Tripiṭaka|en|Taishō Tripiṭaka|WD=Q837315|lt=Taishō Tripiṭaka}} 232).{{citation|url=http://www.acmuller.net/descriptive_catalogue/files/k0010.html|title=The Korean Buddhist Canon: A Descriptive Catalog (T 232)}} This ''sūtra'' contains a dialogue between Mañjuśrī and the Buddha on the One [[:en:Samādhi|Samādhi]] (Skt. ''Ekavyūha Samādhi''). {{ill|Sheng-yen|en|Sheng-yen|WD=Q712896|lt=Sheng-yen}} renders the following teaching of Mañjuśrī, for entering ''samādhi'' naturally through transcendent wisdom: {{quote|Contemplate the five {{ill|Skandha|en|Skandha|WD=Q747858|lt=Skandha}}s as originally empty and quiescent, non-arising, non-perishing, equal, without differentiation. Constantly thus practicing, day or night, whether sitting, walking, standing or lying down, finally one reaches an inconceivable state without any obstruction or form. This is the Samadhi of One Act ({{zh|c=一行三昧|p=Yīxíng sānmèi|labels=no}}).Sheng-Yen, Master (聖嚴法師)(1988). [https://web.archive.org/web/20121011012531/http://ccbs.ntu.edu.tw/FULLTEXT/JR-BJ001/02_10.htm ''Tso-Ch'an''], p.364}} ==Vajrayāna Buddhism== Within [[:en:Vajrayāna|Vajrayāna]] Buddhism, Mañjuśrī is a meditational deity and considered a fully enlightened Buddha. In {{ill|Shingon Buddhism|en|Shingon Buddhism|WD=Q550182|lt=Shingon Buddhism}}, he is one of the {{ill|Thirteen Buddhas|en|Thirteen Buddhas|WD=Q3538361|lt=Thirteen Buddhas}} to whom disciples devote themselves. He figures extensively in many esoteric texts such as the ''[[:en:Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa|Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa]]'' and the ''{{ill|Mañjuśrīnāmasamgīti|en|Mañjuśrīnāmasamgīti|WD=Q3577095|lt=Mañjuśrīnāmasamgīti}}''. His consort in some traditions is [[Saraswati]]. The ''Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa'', which later came to be classified under [[Outer Tantras#Kriyatantra|Kriyātantra]], states that ''mantra''s taught in the [[:en:Śaiva|Śaiva]], Garuḍa, and [[:en:Vaiṣṇava|Vaiṣṇava]] ''tantra''s will be effective if applied by Buddhists since they were all taught originally by Mañjuśrī.Sanderson, Alexis. "The Śaiva Age: The Rise and Dominance of Śaivism during the Early Medieval Period." In: Genesis and Development of Tantrism, edited by Shingo Einoo. Tokyo: Institute of Oriental Culture, University of Tokyo, 2009. Institute of Oriental Culture Special Series, 23, pp. 129-131. ==Iconography== Mañjuśrī is depicted as a male bodhisattva wielding a flaming sword in his right hand, representing the realization of transcendent wisdom which cuts down ignorance and duality. The scripture supported by the [[:en:Padma (attribute)|padma]] (lotus) held in his left hand is a ''Prajñāpāramitā sūtra'', representing his attainment of ultimate realization from the blossoming of wisdom. Mañjuśrī is often depicted as riding or seated on a blue {{ill|Lion|en|Lion|WD=Q140|lt=Lion}}, as can be seen at {{ill|Buddha Tooth Relic Temple and Museum|en|Buddha Tooth Relic Temple and Museum|WD=Q839965|lt=Buddha Tooth Relic Temple and Museum}} in {{ill|Singapore|en|Singapore|WD=Q334|lt=Singapore}}. (see opposite), or sitting on the skin of a lion. This represents the use of wisdom to tame the mind, which is compared to riding or subduing a ferocious lion. In Chinese and Japanese Buddhist art, Mañjuśrī's sword is sometimes replaced with a ''{{ill|Ruyi (scepter)|en|Ruyi (scepter)|WD=Q1448880|lt=ruyi}}'' scepter, especially in representations of his ''{{ill|Vimalakirti Sutra|en|Vimalakirti Sutra|WD=Q110646|lt=Vimalakirti Sutra}}'' discussion with the layman {{ill|Vimalakirti|en|Vimalakirti|WD=Q2502143|lt=Vimalakirti}}.Davidson, J. LeRoy, "The Origin and Early Use of the Ju-i", ''Artibus Asiae'' 1950,13.4, 240. According to {{ill|Berthold Laufer|en|Berthold Laufer|WD=Q71600|lt=Berthold Laufer}}, the first Chinese representation of a ''ruyi'' was in an 8th-century Mañjuśrī painting by {{ill|Wu Daozi|en|Wu Daozi|WD=Q1196022|lt=Wu Daozi}}, showing it held in his right hand taking the place of the usual sword. In subsequent Chinese and Japanese paintings of Buddhas, a ''ruyi'' was occasionally represented as a Padma with a long stem curved like a ''ruyi''.Laufer, Berthold, ''[https://openlibrary.org/books/OL7181158M/Jade Jade, a Study in Chinese Archaeology and Religion]'', Field Museum of Natural History, 1912, 339. He is one of the Four Great Bodhisattvas of {{ill|Chinese Buddhism|en|Chinese Buddhism|WD=Q847618|lt=Chinese Buddhism}}, the other three being {{ill|Kṣitigarbha|en|Kṣitigarbha|WD=Q604687|lt=Kṣitigarbha}}, {{ill|Avalokiteśvara|en|Avalokiteśvara|WD=Q193849|lt=Avalokiteśvara}}, and {{ill|Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|en|Samantabhadra (Bodhisattva)|WD=Q868306|lt=Samantabhadra}}. In China, he is often paired with Samantabhadra{{Citation needed|date=September 2022}}. In {{ill|Tibetan Buddhism|en|Tibetan Buddhism|WD=Q483889|lt=Tibetan Buddhism}}, Mañjuśrī is sometimes depicted in a trinity with Avalokiteśvara and [[:en:Vajrapāṇi|Vajrapāṇi]]{{Citation needed|date=September 2022}}. ==Mantras== === Arapacana mantra === A {{ill|Mantra|en|Mantra|WD=Q131510|lt=Mantra}} commonly associated with Mañjuśrī is the following:Buswell, Robert. Lopez, Donald. ''The Princeton Dictionary of Buddhism.'' 2013. p. 527 :''oṃ arapacana dhīḥ'' The Arapacana is a {{ill|Syllabary|en|Syllabary|WD=Q182133|lt=Syllabary}} consisting of forty-two letters, and is named after the first five letters: ''a, ra, pa, ca, na''.Buswell, Robert. Lopez, Donald. ''The Princeton Dictionary of Buddhism.'' 2013. p. 61 This syllabary was most widely used for the [[:en:Gāndhārī language|Gāndhārī language]] with the {{ill|Kharosthi|en|Kharosthi|WD=Q1161266|lt=Kharoṣṭhī script}} but also appears in some Sanskrit texts. The syllabary features in Mahāyāna texts such as the longer ''[[:en:Prajñāpāramitā|Prajñāpāramitā]]'' texts, the ''[[:en:Gaṇḍavyūha Sūtra|Gaṇḍavyūha Sūtra]]'', the ''{{ill|Lalitavistara Sūtra|en|Lalitavistara Sūtra|WD=Q1381826|lt=Lalitavistara Sūtra}}'', the ''[[:en:Avataṃsaka Sūtra|Avataṃsaka Sūtra]]'', the ''{{ill|Dharmaguptaka|en|Dharmaguptaka|WD=Q2445824|lt=Dharmaguptaka}} {{ill|Vinaya|en|Vinaya|WD=Q848764|lt=Vinaya}}'', and the ''[[:en:Mūlasarvāstivāda|Mūlasarvāstivāda]] Vinaya''. In some of these texts, the Arapacana syllabary serves as a {{ill|Mnemonic|en|Mnemonic|WD=Q191062|lt=Mnemonic}} for important Mahāyāna concepts. Due to its association with him, ''Arapacana'' may even serve as an alternate name for Mañjuśrī. The ''Sutra on Perfect Wisdom'' (Conze 1975) defines the significance of each syllable thus: # ''A'' is a door to the insight that all dharmas are unproduced from the very beginning (''ādya-anutpannatvād''). # ''RA'' is a door to the insight that all dharmas are without dirt (''rajas''). # ''PA'' is a door to the insight that all dharmas have been expounded in the ultimate sense (''paramārtha''). # ''CA'' is a door to the insight that the decrease (''cyavana'') or rebirth of any dharma cannot be apprehended, because all dharmas do not decrease, nor are they reborn. # ''NA'' is a door to the insight that the names (i.e. ''nāma'') of all dharmas have vanished; the essential nature behind names cannot be gained or lost. Tibetan pronunciation is slightly different and so the Tibetan characters read: ''{{IAST|oṃ a ra pa tsa na dhīḥ}}'' ({{bo|w=om a ra pa tsa na d+hIH|t=ༀ་ཨ་ར་པ་ཙ་ན་དྷཱི༔|lang=yes}}).[http://www.visiblemantra.org/manjusri.html] - Visible Mantra's website In Tibetan tradition, this mantra is believed to enhance wisdom and improve one's skills in debating, memory, writing, and other literary abilities. "{{IAST|Dhīḥ}}" is the seed syllable of the mantra and is chanted with greater emphasis and also repeated a number of times as a [[:en:decrescendo|decrescendo]]. === Other mantras === According to the {{ill|Mañjuśrī-mūla-kalpa|en|Mañjuśrī-mūla-kalpa|WD=Q6799169|lt=''Mañjuśrī­mūlakalpa''}}, "the ultimate heart essence of Mañjuśrī, which accomplishes all endeavors" is the following mantra:{{Cite web |title=The Root Manual of the Rites of Mañjuśrī / 84000 Reading Room |url=https://read.84000.co/translation/toh543.html |access-date=2024-03-22 |website=84000 Translating The Words of The Buddha |language=en}}
Namaḥ sarvabuddhānām oṁ maṁ
The ''Sādhanamālā'' also contains a popular mantra which refers to Mañjuśrī as the "lord of speech" (Vāgīśvara):Bhattacharyya, Benoytosh. ''The Indian Buddhist Iconography Mainly Based on the Sādhanamālā and Other Cognate Tāntric Texts of Rituals'' (2nd Ed.)'','' pp. 113, 116. K. L. MUKHOPADHYAY, Calcutta, 1958.
Oṃ Vāgīśvara Mūḥ
This mantra is very popular in {{ill|Nepal|en|Nepal|WD=Q837|lt=Nepal}}, where Vāgīśvara Mañjuśrī is a popular deity. Another Mañjuśrī mantra is the mantra for Mañjuvajra, a tantric form of Mañjuśrī associated with the {{ill|Guhyasamāja Tantra|en|Guhyasamāja Tantra|WD=Q1400398|lt=Guhyasamaja}} tradition, it is:Bhattacharyya, Benoytosh. ''The Indian Buddhist Iconography Mainly Based on the Sādhanamālā and Other Cognate Tāntric Texts of Rituals'' (2nd Ed.)'','' pp. 117. K. L. MUKHOPADHYAY, Calcutta, 1958.
Oṃ Mañjuvajra Hūṃ
==In Buddhist cultures== {{MahayanaBuddhism}} [[File:Yulin Cave 3 w wall Manjusri (Western Xia).jpg|thumb|A painting of the Buddhist ''manjusri'' from the {{ill|Yulin Caves|en|Yulin Caves|WD=Q751622|lt=Yulin Caves}} of {{ill|Gansu|en|Gansu|WD=Q42392|lt=Gansu}}, China, from the {{ill|Tangut people|en|Tangut people|WD=Q756608|lt=Tangut}}-led {{ill|Western Xia|en|Western Xia|WD=Q7427|lt=Western Xia}} dynasty]] ===In China=== Mañjuśrī is known in China as ''Wenshu'' ({{zh|c=文殊|p=Wénshū}}). {{ill|Mount Wutai|en|Mount Wutai|WD=Q120314|lt=Mount Wutai}} in {{ill|Shanxi|en|Shanxi|WD=Q46913|lt=Shanxi}}, one of the four {{ill|Sacred Mountains of China|en|Sacred Mountains of China|WD=Q1062231|lt=Sacred Mountains of China}}, is considered by Chinese Buddhists to be his {{ill|Bodhimaṇḍa|en|Bodhimaṇḍa|WD=Q1939884|lt=Bodhimaṇḍa}}. He was said to bestow spectacular visionary experiences to those on selected mountain peaks and caves there. In Mount Wutai's {{ill|Foguang Temple|en|Foguang Temple|WD=Q44615|lt=Foguang Temple}}, the Manjusri Hall to the right of its main hall was recognized to have been built in 1137 during the {{ill|Jin dynasty (1115–1234)|en|Jin dynasty (1115–1234)|WD=Q5066|lt=Jin dynasty}}. The hall was thoroughly studied, mapped and first photographed by early twentieth-century Chinese architects {{ill|Liang Sicheng|en|Liang Sicheng|WD=Q71874|lt=Liang Sicheng}} and {{ill|Lin Huiyin|en|Lin Huiyin|WD=Q467140|lt=Lin Huiyin}}.Liang, Ssucheng. ''A Pictorial History of Chinese Architecture''. Ed. Wilma Fairbank. Cambridge, Michigan: The MIT Press, 1984. These made it a popular place of pilgrimage, but patriarchs including {{ill|en:Linji Yixuan|en|en:Linji Yixuan|WD=Q326950|lt=en:Linji Yixuan}} and {{ill|Yunmen Wenyan|en|Yunmen Wenyan|WD=Q2165671|lt=Yunmen Wenyan}} declared the mountain off limits.*See Robert M. Gimello, "Chang Shang-ying on Wu-t'ai Shan", in Pilgrims and Sacred Sites in China:, ed. Susan Naquin and Chün-fang Yü (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1992), pp. 89–149; and Steven Heine, "Visions, Divisions, Revisions: The Encounter Between Iconoclasm and Supernaturalism in Kōan Cases about Mount Wu-t'ai", in The Kōan, pp. 137–167. Mount Wutai was also associated with the {{ill|East Mountain Teaching|en|East Mountain Teaching|WD=Q11526728|lt=East Mountain Teaching}}.{{Cite book | last= Heine | first= Steven | title= Opening a Mountain: Koans of the Zen Masters | publisher= Oxford University Press | location= USA | page= [https://archive.org/details/openingmountain00stev/page/ ] | year= 2002 | isbn= 0-19-513586-5 | url-access= registration | url= https://archive.org/details/openingmountain00stev/page/ }} Mañjuśrī has been associated with Mount Wutai since ancient times. Paul Williams writes:Williams, Paul. ''Mahayana Buddhism: The Doctrinal Foundations.'' 2000. p. 227 {{quote|Apparently the association of Mañjuśrī with Wutai (Wu-t'ai) Shan in north China was known in classical times in India itself, identified by Chinese scholars with the mountain in the 'north-east' (when seen from India or {{ill|Central Asia|en|Central Asia|WD=Q27275|lt=Central Asia}}) referred to as the abode of Mañjuśrī in the ''{{ill|Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra|en|Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra|WD=Q790258|lt=Avataṃsaka Sūtra}}''. There are said to have been pilgrimages from India and other Asian countries to Wutai Shan by the seventh century.}} According to official histories from the {{ill|Qing dynasty|en|Qing dynasty|WD=Q8733|lt=Qing dynasty}}, {{ill|Nurhaci|en|Nurhaci|WD=Q311189|lt=Nurhaci}}, a military leader of the {{ill|Jurchen people|en|Jurchen people|WD=Q753880|lt=Jurchens}} of {{ill|Northeast China|en|Northeast China|WD=Q1057925|lt=Northeast China}} and founder of what became the Qing dynasty, named his tribe after Mañjuśrī as the [[:en:Manchus|Manchus]].{{Cite book|last=Agui|title=满洲源流考 (the Origin of Manchus)|publisher=Liaoning Nationality Publishing House|year=1988|isbn=9787805270609|url=http://book.douban.com/subject/4106389/}} The true origin of the name Manchu is disputed.{{Cite book|first=Chongnian|last=Yan|title=明亡清兴六十年 (彩图珍藏版)|publisher=Zhonghua Book Company|year=2008|isbn=9787101059472|url=http://book.douban.com/subject/2359481/}} Monk {{ill|Hanshan (poet)|en|Hanshan (poet)|WD=Q930333|lt=Hanshan}} ({{lang|zh|寒山}}) is widely considered to be a metaphorical manifestation of Mañjuśrī. He is known for having co-written the following famous poem about reincarnation with monk {{ill|Shide (monk)|en|Shide (monk)|WD=Q752964|lt=Shide}}:{{cite web|url=http://foxue.163.com/photonew/B06C0324/114.html|title=诗僧寒山与拾得:文殊菩萨普贤菩萨化身|publisher=NetEase Buddhism Channel|date=2014-12-10|language=zh|location=Beijing}}{{cite web|url=http://www.lingshh.com/wuyuefojiao/hantingjie.htm|title=寒山诗赏析|author=韩廷杰|publisher=灵山海会期刊社|language=zh|location=Zhejiang}} {{poem quote|Drumming your grandpa in the shrine, Cooking your aunts in the pot, Marrying your grandma in the past, Should I laugh or not? {{lang|zh-Hant|堂上打鼓打公皮， 鍋內煎煮是姑娘， 三世祖母娶為婦， 我今不笑等何時。}}}} In {{ill|Tibetan Buddhism|en|Tibetan Buddhism|WD=Q483889|lt=Tibetan Buddhism}}, Mañjuśrī manifests in a number of different {{ill|Tantra|en|Tantra|WD=Q181510|lt=Tantric}} forms. {{ill|Yamantaka|en|Yamantaka|WD=Q1348317|lt=Yamāntaka}} (meaning 'terminator of {{ill|Yama|en|Yama|WD=Q45097|lt=Yama}} i.e. Death') is the [[:en:Wrathful deity|wrathful]] manifestation of Mañjuśrī, popular within the {{ill|Gelug|en|Gelug|WD=Q319218|lt=Gelug}} school of Tibetan Buddhism. Other variations upon his traditional form as Mañjuśrī include {{ill|Mañjuśrīnāmasamgīti|en|Mañjuśrīnāmasamgīti|WD=Q3577095|lt=Namasangiti}}, Arapacana Manjushri, etc. In Tibetan Buddhism, Mañjuśrī is also an ''{{ill|Yidam|en|Yidam|WD=Q2072049|lt=Yidam}}''. The {{ill|Emperor Manjushri|en|Emperor Manjushri|WD=Q11080008|lt=Emperor Manjushri}} as a honorific title was also given to Qing emperors such as the {{ill|Qianlong Emperor|en|Qianlong Emperor|WD=Q19133|lt=Qianlong Emperor}}. In the Taoist pantheon, Mañjuśrī is adopted as a Taoist deity known as {{ill|Wenshu Guangfa Tianzun|en|Wenshu Guangfa Tianzun|WD=Q7982957|lt=Wenshu Guangfa Tianzun}}. This deity appears in the Ming Dynasty novel ''[[:en:Fengshen Yanyi|Fengshen Yanyi]]'' as a senior disciple of {{ill|Yuanshi Tianzun|en|Yuanshi Tianzun|WD=Q1195885|lt=Yuanshi Tianzun}}, the highest deity in Taoism. However, the books ''Qunxian Xianpo Tianmen'' and ''Western Tang Dynasty Biography'' state that Wenshu Guangfa Tianzun and Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva are not the same person.{{cite book |title=四川道敎史话 [Sichuan Taoist History]|date=1985 |publisher=四川人民出版社 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vrwEAQAAIAAJ&q=%E6%96%87%E6%AE%8A%E5%B9%BF%E6%B3%95%E5%A4%A9%E5%B0%8A |quote=... 文殊广法天尊,就是文殊,至于观音,改名叫作慈航道人,自称“贫道乃灵鹫山元觉洞燃灯道人”者,前身就是燃灯佛,西方极乐世界的孔雀明王,成了准提道人。|language=zh}}{{cite book |title=当代 |date=2009 |publisher=人民文学出版社 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iRJMAQAAIAAJ&q=%E6%96%87%E6%AE%8A%E5%B9%BF%E6%B3%95%E5%A4%A9%E5%B0%8A|quote=... 文殊广法天尊” ,这与三教中的大师法号习惯带“子” ,如“广成子” “云中子” “赤精子”也大异其趣。却不可认为这位“文殊”便真是佛家那位“文殊菩萨” [Translation:... Wenshu Guangfa Tianzun," this differs significantly from the usual naming conventions for masters in the Three Religions, where they typically include "Zi" (子) in their titles, such as "Guangcheng Zi," "Yunzhong Zi," "Chijing Zi," and others. However, it should not be assumed that this "Wenshu" is indeed the same as the Buddhist figure "Manjushri Bodhisattva."] |language=zh}} ({{ill|East Java|en|East Java|WD=Q3586|lt=East Java}}, {{ill|Indonesia|en|Indonesia|WD=Q252|lt=Indonesia}}), probably made in 1823 by J.Th. Bik in Batavia.]] ===In Nepal=== According to {{ill|Swayambhu Purana|en|Swayambhu Purana|WD=Q7654077|lt=Swayambhu Purana}}, the {{ill|Kathmandu Valley|en|Kathmandu Valley|WD=Q970717|lt=Kathmandu Valley}} was once a lake. It is believed that Mañjuśrī came on a pilgrimage from his earthly abode-[[:en:Wutaishan|Wutaishan]] (five-peaked mountain) in China. He saw a lotus flower in the center of the lake, which emitted brilliant radiance. He cut a gorge at Chovar with his flaming sword to allow the lake to drain. The place where the lotus flower settled became the great {{ill|Swayambhunath|en|Swayambhunath|WD=Q12946982|lt=Swayambhunath}} Stupa, and the valley thus became habitable. ===In Indonesia=== In eighth century {{ill|Java|en|Java|WD=Q3757|lt=Java}} during the [[:en:Mataram Kingdom|Mataram Kingdom]], Mañjuśrī was a prominent deity revered by the [[:en:Sailendra dynasty|Sailendra dynasty]], patrons of Mahayana Buddhism. The {{ill|Kelurak inscription|en|Kelurak inscription|WD=Q4263126|lt=Kelurak inscription}} (782) and {{ill|Manjusrigrha inscription|en|Manjusrigrha inscription|WD=Q10991107|lt=Manjusrigrha inscription}} (792) mentioned about the construction of a grand Prasada named ''Vajrāsana Mañjuśrīgṛha'' (Vajra House of Mañjuśrī) identified today as {{ill|Sewu|en|Sewu|WD=Q2936254|lt=Sewu}} temple, located just 800 meters north of the {{ill|Prambanan|en|Prambanan|WD=Q47721|lt=Prambanan}}. Sewu is the second largest Buddhist temple in Central Java after {{ill|Borobudur|en|Borobudur|WD=Q42798|lt=Borobudur}}. The depiction of Mañjuśrī in Sailendra art is similar to those of the {{ill|Pala Empire|en|Pala Empire|WD=Q668412|lt=Pala Empire}} style of [[:en:Nalanda|Nalanda]], {{ill|Bihar|en|Bihar|WD=Q1165|lt=Bihar}}. Mañjuśrī was portrayed as a youthful handsome man with the palm of his hands tattooed with the image of a flower. His right hand is facing down with an open palm while his left-hand holds an ''utpala'' (blue lotus). He also uses the necklace made of tiger {{ill|canine tooth|en|canine tooth|WD=Q19625|lt=canine teeth}}. ==Gallery== File:Hermitage hall 342 - 03.jpg|Mañjuśrī figure from [[:en:Candi Jago|Candi Jago]], 14th century Java, Indonesia. File:WLA ima Manjusri.jpg|Mañjuśrī figure brandishing sword of wisdom in {{ill|Nepal|en|Nepal|WD=Q837|lt=Nepal}} File:Astasahasrika Prajnaparamita Manjusri Bodhisattva.jpeg|Palm leaf manuscript painting of Mañjuśrī. [[:en:Nalanda|Nalanda]], {{ill|Bihar|en|Bihar|WD=Q1165|lt=Bihar}}, India. File:COLLECTIE TROPENMUSEUM Zilveren Manjusri beeld afkomstig uit Ngemplak Semongan TMnr 10016132.jpg|Silver figure of Mañjuśrī holding a long-stemmed lotus. Central Java, Indonesia.
